title.value: An Analysis of Phase Behavior and Displacement Characteristics of Multicomponent Mixtures

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: Cubic equations of state are widely used in the petroleum industry for characterizing fluids. Even though cubic equations of state do a good job of characterizing fluid phase behavior, currently there is no simple method available that either looks at the effects of individual components on the phase behavior of a complex mixture (made up of large number of components of different chemical types) or that can help us understand how different components would behave relative to each other as the composition of the mixture changes.Here a novel approach to look at these problems is presented. This approach is based on a two-step minimization of Gibbs energy which reveals some new characteristics of two-parameter equations of state, such as the Peng-Robinson equation of state (EOS). First, the ideal part of Gibbs energy is minimized subject to certain constraints that include the mixing rules for EOS parameters. A second minimization is performed over the total Gibbs energy with the Lagrange multipliers from the first minimization as a reduced set of variables. This two-step minimization ofGibbs energy has been successfully used earlier (Kaul and Thrasher 1996) in formulating parameter-based algorithms for phase equilibrium predictions. The two-step minimization approach provides simple and linear expressions for equilibrium constants and the variables in these expressions have some special properties. These features have been exploited in the work undertaken here, to determine, without detailed phase behavior computations, how K-values of different components are ordered among themselves and how components of different chemical types influence the phase behavior of petroleum mixtures.Using this novel approach, this work demonstrates that there is an additional loss of physics, besides the expected loss of information, when large systems such as crude oils are characterized in terms of just a few pseudocomponents. It is also shown that the presence of different chemical types in the petroleum mixtures influences the phase envelop in such a manner that the phase behavior may not be adequately represented even by a single carbon number representation of these mixtures. Available literature on compositional description of reservoir fluids was examined with these issues in mind, and studies were undertaken on both synthetic and real petroleum mixtures to analyze phase behavior of these mixtures under static and displacement conditions.While a reasonable phase behavior match (under static conditions) for the synthetic mixtures studied could be achieved by a few pseudocomponent representations, the displacement studies on these mixtures to simulate dry gas recycling in a condensate reservoir and the near miscible displacement of an oil revealed that there is considerable spreading of saturation fronts for mixtures made up of a large number of components. Such behavior is not captured accurately by pseudocomponent representations and, as a result, there may be significant errors in recoveries even when a reasonable match with the PVT (pressure, volume and temperature) behavior of the full representation has been achieved. The sensitivity of the displacement behavior to the characterization also brings out the importance of displacement experiments to characterize petroleum mixtures adequately.Phase behavior-related problems are also studied here through the topology of ruled surfaces. In terms of the topology of a ruled surface, it may be said that there are two levels of information that are lost due to pseudocomponent characterization. One level of information has to do with the coarsening of component properties. While it may not be difficult to mimic recovery behavior with a few pseudocomponents, given a displacement behavior at a particular pressure, it is not possible to represent saturation profiles accurately with six to eight pseudocomponents. This is because fluid characterization with few components introduces large steps (shocks) in the saturation profiles. The other level of information that is lost is due to the dependence of the solution structure for displacement of complex mixtures (made of different chemical types) on pressure (the ordering of saturation fronts may change with pressure). For these mixtures, it may be difficult to mimic, with a few pseudocomponents, the consequences of the pressure dependence of solution structures on recovery behavior. A non-trivial and a problem-specific approach needs to be adopted in such situations; one such approach is discussed here.
